strengths: Composed person retrieval is a useful application of multimodal retrieval. The 1.15-million-triplet SynCPR training set and manually annotated ITCPR benchmark could provide valuable resources for studying transfer from synthetic images to real person images.

The paired-image generation pipeline is practical and clearly motivated. Generating both views together, varying LoRA strength, and filtering multimodal consistency form a coherent approach to reducing annotation requirements.

The reported improvements include meaningful comparisons using the same training data: FAFA achieves 46.54% Rank-1 versus SPRC’s 42.27% on ITCPR. The additional CIRR results, 54.48% versus 51.96%, provide evidence of usefulness beyond the proposed benchmark.
The paper is generally understandable. Component ablations, generation prompts, optimization settings, and the gallery reannotation procedure provide useful implementation and evaluation detail.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is not convincingly held out. Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 select the filtering threshold, feature-selection parameters, loss weights, and masking ratio using performance on ITCPR, which Appendix B.1.3 describes as exclusively a test set. No separate validation split is documented. This creates substantial scope for test-set overfitting and weakens comparisons with baselines using their originally recommended settings.

The central claims of high-quality, identity-consistent synthetic data lack independent validation. There is no human audit reporting identity errors, caption correctness, or agreement with the automated judge. Averaging four quality scores can retain a sample with poor identity consistency if its other scores are high. Qualitative examples and downstream accuracy support usefulness, but do not establish the claimed quality or comprehensive demographic coverage.

Important contributions of the synthesis pipeline are not isolated quantitatively. The paper does not report controlled downstream comparisons for joint versus independent image generation, generator fine-tuning versus no fine-tuning, or varying LoRA strength versus a fixed strength. Consequently, the necessity and individual benefits of these design choices remain unclear.

FAFA combines established BLIP-2 representations with top-k similarity aggregation, distribution matching, diversity regularization, and feature reconstruction. Its relationship to prior fine-grained alignment methods needs sharper treatment. Table 2 compares the combined FDA mechanism against ITC without separately isolating aggregation, distribution matching, and group-based soft labels. No uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of smaller gains, such as MFR’s additional 0.49 Rank-1 and 0.11 mAP points over FDA+FD.

The unimodal and score-fusion comparisons use different training data and do not replace equally trained image-only and text-only FAFA controls. Such controls would clarify whether the model learns complementary composition beyond domain adaptation. Reporting results separately for ITCPR’s three source datasets would also make the claimed generalization easier to assess.

Reproduction and dataset documentation remain incomplete despite the useful appendix: the reconstruction decoder and batch sampling needed for group-based supervision are insufficiently specified, and annotation agreement and residual false-negative rates are unreported. Source-data reuse terms and privacy considerations also deserve documentation because real person images support both generator fine-tuning and evaluation. The recommendation is driven primarily by the evaluation and data-validation shortcomings.
